As we celebrate Women's History Month, we remember Hazel Raines. She the first woman in the state of Georgia to earn a pilot’s license. Raised here in Macon and a graduate of Wesleyan College, she earned both a private and commercial pilot’s license.

Raines became one of only twenty-five women chosen to fly with the British Air Transport Auxiliary (ATA) during World War II, flying damaged aircraft back to repair stations. During the war, she logged the most flight hours of any ATA pilot and survived a plane crash.

She continued her dedication and service to the U.S. military in 1950, when she was the first female reserve pilot called into active service for the Korean War.

She overcame asthma, a heart condition, and many other obstacles to achieve her goals. After her death at the young age of forty, Raines was dubbed “Georgia’s First Lady of Flight” and was inducted into the Georgia Women of Achievement in 1995.

Today, TSA personnel are missing their first full paychecks - thanks to Chuck Schumer and the caucus he leads. But what is ironic is that not one Senate Democrat who voted to deny paychecks for others has missed their own. 

I am so tired of politicians making a political point at the expense of the men and women who show up every single day to do their jobs and keep Americans safe. For a party that once resoundingly lectured against the dangers of a government shutdown, their current posture is as hypocritical as it is irresponsible. Senate Democrats have hijacked appropriations and shutdowns as their catchall for political leverage. 

But let me be clear: while that approach may serve their far-Left base and campaign strategy, it does nothing to safeguard the nation or support the personnel who carry out these missions everyday.

My statement on the House passage of my bill to end the Democrat shutdown and fully fund Homeland Security:

The Constitution places the safety and security of the American people at the center of the federal government’s responsibilities. It is a duty I don’t take lightly. Amidst rising global tensions and natural disaster possibilities, jeopardizing security operations and emergency preparedness is the last thing anyone should be doing. Yet, Democrats have kept the Department of Homeland Security shuttered for weeks – and again voted to keep it that way.

They are actively choosing to deny resources to the very people responsible for protecting the American homeland. Cybersecurity operations are at limited capacity, as adversaries like Iran, Russia, and China seek to exploit infrastructure vulnerabilities. Training for first responders has been canceled. FEMA grants – utilized by state and local entities to ensure safety and combat terrorism – can’t be accessed. TSA officers are being forced to work through the shutdown while missing paychecks. Coast Guard men and women, including those in harm’s way in Bahrain, are completing missions without full resources behind them. Even security preparations to keep attendees safe at the America 250 celebrations, the FIFA World Cup, the LA2028 Olympics, and more face disruptions. These impacts are not political or hyperbole. They are the direct cost of Democrats’ decision to play politics with the safeguards of this country.

My priority is serving and protecting Oklahomans and all Americans, which is why I voted again today to pass full-year DHS funding. No selective resourcing – full operational funding for the Department of Homeland Security and the personnel who stand watch over this nation every day. Despite bipartisan majorities in both chambers, a small minority of Democrats continue to hold this funding hostage. However, let me be clear: shielding the homeland should never be treated as a political bargaining chip.

We in Congress can debate the merits of the War Powers Act, but the hard reality is that the President has committed U.S. troops to active engagement in combat with an enemy that has targeted and killed Americans for decades. We have lost six soldiers in this fight with the potential for more casualties. What our troops need now is for our Congress, and this country, to know that they are supported. It is for this reason that I oppose Senator Kaine’s War Powers Resolution—based on the practical implications of its passage.

As written, it requires removal of troops from hostilities, leaving no room for operations that have already started to reach an even partially successful conclusion to degrade Iran’s nuclear capabilities. As Iran attacks everything it can, from military bases to embassies to civilian targets, we cannot tie our military’s hands or abruptly leave our allies and partners to fight on their own.

There is no question that the President should have sought authorization from Congress before striking Iran on this scale, likewise bringing in our allies ahead of time as they now are equally in danger. P000597.text:
RT by @chelliepingree: 🚨 FARM BILL POWER GRAB

The 2026 Farm Bill quietly slipped in three sections that could shield pesticide companies from lawsuits, block states from regulating chemicals, and weaken water protections nationwide.

Rep. Chellie Pingree just introduced an amendment to delete them entirely.

Here’s the plain-English breakdown everyone should understand 👇

1. Lawsuit Shield for Pesticide Companies (Section 10205)

If this stays in the bill, chemical companies could avoid liability even if new evidence shows their product causes cancer or neurological damage. As long as the pesticide followed the label approved under Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA), victims may lose the ability to sue.

Why this matters:

Bayer has already paid about $11 billion to settle lawsuits over the herbicide Glyphosate linked to non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma. More than 165,000 claims have been filed against Bayer tied to the product Roundup herbicide.

If Section 10205 passes, future cases like those could be blocked.

Pingree’s amendment removes that shield.

2. States Lose Power Over Pesticide Rules (Section 10206)

Right now states and local governments can create stricter pesticide protections than the federal government.

That includes things like bans on spraying near schools or buffer zones around homes and waterways.

Section 10206 would override those rules nationwide.

That reverses precedent set by the Supreme Court case
Wisconsin Public Intervenor v. Mortier, which affirmed that local governments can regulate pesticides.

Seven states currently allow local pesticide control.
Those protections could disappear overnight.

3. Weakened Water & Wildlife Protections (Section 10207)

This provision would exempt pesticides from additional review under major environmental laws including the Clean Water Act and the Endangered Species Act.

In practice that means pesticides approved by EPA could enter rivers, streams, and habitats without additional permits or environmental review.

Government monitoring has already detected pesticide residues in most U.S. waterways, raising concerns about runoff impacts on fish, wildlife, and drinking water.

Why This Fight Is Exploding

Critics argue the provisions protect chemical manufacturers, override state authority, and weaken environmental oversight.

Supporters claim the sections reduce litigation risk, simplify national pesticide regulation, and protect agricultural production.

Pingree’s amendment simply removes the three sections entirely, restoring the existing regulatory framework.

What Happens Next

The bill is still in markup inside the House Agriculture Committee.

That means these provisions can still be removed before the Farm Bill moves forward.

This fight will determine who controls pesticide rules in America — communities or chemical companies.

Key Takeaways

The Farm Bill includes three provisions that could shield pesticide companies from lawsuits.

They could also strip states and towns of authority to regulate pesticide use locally.

Environmental protections tied to waterways and wildlife could be weakened.

The Pingree amendment would remove those provisions entirely and restore current law. @amtoxicology @chelliepingree

Thursday's attack at Temple Israel — the nation's largest Reform synagogue—is an attack on all Americans.

Statement on yesterday's attack from the 21 members of the Congressional Jewish Caucus:

Horrified and heartbroken by today’s attack at Temple Israel in West Bloomfield, Michigan, where an armed assailant rammed a truck into the synagogue and opened fire while children were inside the building’s early childhood center.

Thanks to the heroic actions of the synagogue’s security team, the attacker was stopped and families are able to hold their children tonight. I’m deeply grateful that no children, staff, or congregants were killed or injured, and I wish the injured security officer a swift recovery.

This attack was meant to terrorize a Jewish community at prayer and is one of several attacks targeting Jewish houses of worship across North America in recent weeks. No parent should have to wonder if their child is safe at preschool. No congregation should have to fear gathering to pray.

We cannot accept or normalize antisemitic violence. I stand with the congregation of Temple Israel and with Jewish communities everywhere.

Last year, I was proud to deliver historic wins for American agriculture through passage of the One Big Beautiful Bill — strengthening the farm safety net with a historic $66 billion investment, boosting reference prices and crop insurance, promoting trade, and securing long-overdue SNAP reforms.

This week, we’re building on that success with the 2026 Farm Bill.

This year’s Farm Bill authorizes the remaining agriculture programs not included in H.R. 1 and advances key provisions I’ve fought for — including my USDA CROP Act to give producers a stronger voice in pesticide decisions and a pilot crop insurance program that will incentivize farmers to bring their cotton to harvest. It strengthens trade promotion, supports new farmers, invests in conservation and precision agriculture, and continues holding states accountable for SNAP mismanagement.

After years of Farm Bill inaction — with Democrats holding our farmers hostage to protect bloated and broken welfare programs — we changed the equation. S001215.text:
Our worst fears came to West Bloomfield today. To the congregants of Temple Israel and Jewish families across our community and beyond, we stand with you in horror of the reality that Jewish Americans confront every time they enter a place of worship, attend a community event, or gather with loved ones.

Michiganders’ lives were saved today by the heroism of security officials on site and the speed of Oakland County’s first responders. Thanks to their bravery and quick actions, Temple Israel’s congregants, staff, and students are alive and safe tonight in their homes. Our community forever owes a debt to the men and women who kept this synagogue safe, and we all send our prayers to the wounded security guard who is recovering in the hospital.

It should not be like this. Jewish families should never have to fear gathering at a synagogue, sending their children to religious school, or simply practicing their faith. Americans should not have to be surrounded by armed guards every time they pray.

It is no longer enough for our leaders to condemn antisemitism. It must be rooted out everywhere. There are things Congress can and must do legislatively—first and foremost, funding every effort we can to keep the Jewish community safe and protect houses of worship—but we must also commit to ending the scourge of antisemitism in every community.

Enough is enough. The congregants of Temple Israel deserve better.

Before our very eyes, a Temple in West Bloomfield is under attack. Like many of you, I am getting reports in real time. To everyone in Michigan’s 11th district, continue to follow the guidance of local law enforcement. 

To the Jewish American community in Michigan and beyond, we stand with you.

Witnesses described past schemes involving straw buyers and shell corporations used to conceal property ownership, as well as evidence uncovered during federal investigations into financial misconduct tied to numerous housing operations.
 
While certain individuals connected to these schemes have been prosecuted, questions remain about whether full accountability has been achieved. Stabilizing the housing authority will require stronger coordination and clearer communication from HUD, along with support to help restore proper management and oversight.
 
Republicans in Congress will continue oversight over federal housing programs to ensure these programs are managed responsibly and that the well-being of residents and taxpayers is top of mind.

Today, I voted against a War Powers Resolution that would have forced an immediate end of military operations in Iran. Here's the full statement I just sent to press: 

The president has not provided sufficient clarity for why this action was necessary at this exact moment. But servicemembers are actively engaged in hostilities, our allies are under attack and the Iranian regime is more desperate than ever to reassert its power. While I do not believe that an abrupt about-face is a good course of action given the reality on the ground, that should not be construed as my approval. While conflict requires that we remain flexible to shifting circumstances, at this time I would not support Congressional authorization or funding for sustained combat operations.

The president has so far acted within the authorities given to him by Congress through the War Powers Act of 1973. He has been briefing Congress, and he has 60 days to make his case for ongoing operations. This is not an illegal war — but it could become one. 

There are reasonable constraints Congress should impose. I urge my colleagues to join me in passing the Resolution I have introduced with Congressman Josh Gottheimer, which would cut the president’s authorized timeline for military action to 30 days and prohibit the deployment of ground troops outside the context of search-and-rescue or intelligence gathering. A month is plenty of time for the president to make his case to the American people — and for Congress to weigh in.

I wrote an op-ed laying out the success of Memphis Safe Task Force in the @DailyMemphian.  
 
“Embedded in the fabric of Tennessee is a spirit of independence, courage, and determination. Tennesseans don’t wait for others to solve our problems. We take challenges head‑on and make things work. That is exactly what we did in Memphis to address violent crime that has plagued the city for too long. 
 
I’ve wrestled with the crime in Memphis since I served as Economic and Community Development Commissioner (ECD) of Tennessee. At that time, we were recruiting a company to bring high-paying jobs to the state and while the company was going to be located hours away from Memphis, its leadership worried about how crime in the city would affect their ability to recruit talent statewide. The CEO asked—quietly—whether the state could provide crime statistics that excluded Memphis to make relocation recruitment easier.
 
With President Trump’s re-election, I saw that opportunity and went fast to work organizing federal, state and local allies to move quietly and effectively to empower law enforcement to do their jobs. 
 
This effort was as broad as it was deep. The Departments of Justice, Housing and Urban Development, Treasury, and most impressively our own Tennessee National Guard collaborated with local authorities to create an atmosphere of calm and justice.
 
As of March 4, 2026, the operation in Memphis has resulted in 6,748 arrests and 1,095 illegal firearms removed from the streets. Those numbers represent thousands of hours of police work, federal coordination, and officers putting themselves in harm’s way to protect their communities.
 
But the true measure of success goes beyond arrest numbers. Violent crime is down. Repeat offenders are being taken off the streets. Displaced children are returning home. Criminal networks that once operated in the open are being dismantled. And for the first time in years, residents and businesses alike are seeing sustained, visible enforcement from all levels of government. Law enforcement is being allowed to do what they do best: keep people safe.”

Read the full op-ed here: https://www.hagerty.senate.gov/op-eds/2026/03/10/senator-hagerty-on-making-memphis-the-safest-city-in-america/

Today, I join the nation in mourning the passing of Dr. Norman C. Francis. For generations of Louisianans, and for people across this country, he represented what steady, faithful leadership in education truly looks like.
 
During his nearly five decades leading Xavier University of Louisiana, Dr. Francis helped transform the institution into a national model of academic excellence and opportunity, especially for students pursuing careers in medicine, science, and public service. His leadership opened doors for countless young people and strengthened the legacy of historically black colleges and universities across our nation. 
 
What made Dr. Francis so remarkable was not only his accomplishments, but his quiet strength, humility, and his belief in the power of education to change lives. Louisiana has lost a historic force for education and opportunity, but the impact of Dr. Francis’ life and work will continue to be felt for generations to come.

Reverend Jesse Jackson stood with the forgotten, spoke for those pushed to the margins, and challenged America, time and time again, to live up to its highest ideals.

As a young person, I had the honor of supporting Reverend Jackson’s historic presidential campaign and witnessed firsthand the faith, courage, and moral clarity that defined his leadership. Over the years, I came to know not only the power of his public voice, but the strength of his personal example. His influence helped shape my own commitment to service and the ongoing work of a more just nation.

I am deeply grateful for his legacy that is not only written in history books, but living on in the people he shaped and the work that we are all blessed to continue because he chose to serve.

My thoughts and prayers are with the entire Jackson family, and all those who are grieving this profound loss today. The greatest way we can honor Reverend Jackson is by carrying forward his historic impact through the continued work for justice and equality for all.

On this day in 1923, Colonel Joe Madison Jackson, an American hero, was born in Newnan, Georgia.

After graduating from Newnan High School, Joe enlisted in the U.S. Army Air Corps, the predecessor of the U.S. Air Force.

Eventually earning the rank of Colonel, Joe Jackson served with distinction in World War II, the Korean War, and the Vietnam War. 

During the Battle of Kham Duc of the Vietnam War in 1968, Colonel Jackson demonstrated extraordinary courage by flying his aircraft through intense enemy fire to rescue three stranded servicemen.  For his bravery during that mission, Colonel Jackson was presented the Medal of Honor by President Lyndon B. Johnson on January 16, 1969. 

Colonel Jackson retired from the U.S. Air Force in 1974 after more than 33 years of honorable service to our Country.

Colonel Jackson will forever be remembered as one of the greatest Americans from Georgia’s 3rd Congressional District!
